title: Bilious vomiting in a neonate: malrotation and midgut volvulus

header.contentArea: Paediatric surgery: the neonate with bilious vomiting

related.why: Non-bilious projectile vomiting in an infant: pyloric stenosis

brief.role: Core surgical trainee on the paediatric surgical team
brief.scenario: Baby Noah Carrick, a boy born at term three days ago, fed well until this morning. He has since vomited green fluid three times. He passed meconium on day one. The neonatal team has asked for a surgical opinion. The examiner will read out examination, blood and imaging findings.
brief.task: Answer the examiner's questions on your assessment, investigation and management. Imaging findings will be read out to you.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Green vomit in a neonate is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise; the gut is on a clock.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Calling it feed intolerance, or sending a shocked baby for imaging.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Bilious vomiting in a neonate is a surgical emergency: I'd treat this as volvulus until proven otherwise."

grid.label: Recognise the emergency
grid.fail: Calls it reflux or feed intolerance and changes the milk.
grid.pass: Malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise; urgent senior paediatric surgical review at a surgical centre.
grid.high: Lists other surgical causes (atresia, Hirschsprung's, meconium ileus) and says a normal examination and plain film do not exclude malrotation.

grid.label: Resuscitate and decompress
grid.fail: Continues feeds or omits a nasogastric tube.
grid.pass: Nil by mouth; nasogastric tube on free drainage; IV access, blood gas, glucose, bloods, cross-match; IV fluids and antibiotics.
grid.high: If shocked: 10–20 mL/kg glucose-free isotonic crystalloid over under 10 minutes, then reassess; maintain glucose.

grid.label: Choose the investigation
grid.fail: Waits for imaging in a shocked, peritonitic baby.
grid.pass: Stable: urgent upper GI contrast study. Shocked or peritonitic: straight to laparotomy without imaging.
grid.high: Knows contrast sensitivity for malrotation is about 96%, and false negatives occur; ultrasound (whirlpool sign) is used where expertise exists.

grid.label: Interpret the contrast findings
grid.fail: Calls it normal or pyloric stenosis.
grid.pass: Duodenojejunal flexure lies right of the midline and low; with volvulus, the duodenum spirals (corkscrew) or is obstructed.
grid.high: States the normal flexure lies left of the left vertebral pedicle at the level of the duodenal bulb.

grid.label: Explain the pathology
grid.fail: Cannot explain why the bowel twists.
grid.pass: Incomplete rotation leaves a narrow mesenteric base, so the midgut twists round the superior mesenteric vessels; Ladd's bands cross the duodenum.
grid.high: Normal rotation is 270 degrees anticlockwise; volvulus usually twists clockwise, so derotation is anticlockwise.

grid.label: Ladd's procedure
grid.pass: Laparotomy, anticlockwise derotation, divide Ladd's bands, widen the mesentery, appendicectomy, small bowel to the right and colon to the left.
grid.high: If viability is doubtful, plans a second look rather than a massive resection; warns parents about short bowel syndrome.

high.text: What do you think is going on?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Volvulus until proven otherwise. Other causes include atresia, Hirschsprung's and meconium ileus, but a normal examination and plain film don't exclude malrotation.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Glucose-free isotonic crystalloid, 10 to 20 mL/kg over under 10 minutes, reassess, and keep his glucose up. He then goes to theatre without further imaging.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: What does the contrast study offer?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Sensitivity for malrotation is about 96%, but false negatives happen. Where there's expertise, ultrasound can show the whirlpool sign.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Left of the left vertebral pedicle, at the level of the duodenal bulb.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Normal rotation is 270 degrees anticlockwise. The volvulus usually twists clockwise, so I derotate anticlockwise.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The bowel looks dusky after derotation.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd warm it and plan a second look rather than resect a lot now, and I'd warn his parents about the risk of short bowel syndrome.

failures.move: Treating green vomit as feed intolerance.
failures.consequence: The midgut infarcts while the baby is observed.

failures.move: Sending a shocked, peritonitic baby for a contrast study.
failures.consequence: Delays surgery for a diagnosis already made clinically.

failures.move: No nasogastric tube and continued feeds.
Extensive resection of dusky bowel at first look.

recovery.line: My working diagnosis is volvulus, because missing it costs the whole midgut; I'd then consider atresia and Hirschsprung's.
Turn it anticlockwise, like turning back the hands of a clock.

knowledge.fact: In a prospective audit, 38% of neonates with bilious vomiting had a surgical cause; one malrotation had a normal examination and plain film.
Upper GI contrast: sensitivity 96% for surgically confirmed malrotation.
Normal duodenojejunal flexure: left of the left vertebral pedicle, at the level of the duodenal bulb.
Term neonate needing resuscitation: 10–20 mL/kg glucose-free crystalloid over under 10 minutes.
Ladd's: derotate anticlockwise, divide bands, widen mesentery, appendicectomy.

recall.think: Midgut volvulus can infarct the whole small bowel within hours.
recall.say: "Bilious vomiting in a neonate is volvulus until proven otherwise."
do: Nil by mouth, NG tube, IV fluids
Contrast study if stable; theatre if shocked

partner.opening: You've been asked to see Baby Noah. What do you think is going on?

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks for observations and examination
reveals.finding: HR 150, CRT 2 seconds, pink, alert. Abdomen soft, mildly full, not tender. Green aspirate in the cot.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks for a gas and glucose
Candidate asks for a plain abdominal film
reveals.finding: Read out: the supine abdominal film shows a distended, gas-filled stomach with only sparse gas in the distal bowel.

Read out: the frontal view of the upper GI contrast study shows contrast filling the stomach and passing into the duodenum. The duodenum does not cross the midline: the duodenojejunal flexure lies to the right of the spine and below the level of the duodenal bulb. The proximal jejunum descends on the right in a tight spiral, like a corkscrew.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks what is found at laparotomy
reveals.finding: Midgut volvulus, two turns clockwise; bowel dusky, improves after derotation.

push.question: What is your working diagnosis?
push.expect: Malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise.

push.question: What would you do immediately?
push.expect: Nil by mouth, NG tube, IV access, bloods, fluids, antibiotics, senior call.

push.question: Which investigation, and when would you skip it?
push.expect: Upper GI contrast if stable; theatre if shocked or peritonitic.

push.question: Interpret these contrast study findings.
push.expect: Flexure right of midline and low; corkscrew.

push.question: Why does malrotation lead to volvulus?
push.expect: Narrow mesenteric base; twists round the superior mesenteric vessels.

push.question: Describe Ladd's procedure.
push.expect: Derotate anticlockwise, divide bands, widen mesentery, appendicectomy.

curveballs.prompt: HR 190, mottled, abdomen distended and tender, blood per rectum.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Established volvulus with ischaemia: resuscitate and go straight to theatre, no imaging.

curveballs.prompt: The plain abdominal film is normal. Can he go back to feeds?
curveballs.safeAnswer: No: a normal film does not exclude malrotation; he needs a contrast study.
It ends up on the left after Ladd's, so later appendicitis would be hard to diagnose.
